question: We have two tests to diagnose a serious prognosis disease. Test A has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 60% and test B has a sensitivity of 70% and a specificity of 99%. We have an effective treatment but that produces important adverse effects and also has a very high cost. What test would we choose to make the diagnosis?

options.opa: Test A because it will detect less false positives.
options.opb: Test A because it has a higher sensitivity.
options.opc: Test B because it will detect more false positives.
options.opd: Test A because it will detect more false negatives.
options.ope: Test B because it has a greater specificity.

analysis: In this scenario, we have to consider the implications of sensitivity and specificity in relation to the disease's serious prognosis and the treatment's adverse effects. Test A has a higher sensitivity (95%), meaning it is better at correctly identifying those with the disease, which is crucial given the serious nature of the disease. However, it has a lower specificity (60%), leading to more false positives. Test B, on the other hand, has a lower sensitivity (70%) but a much higher specificity (99%), which means it is better at correctly identifying those without the disease, thus reducing false positives. Given that the treatment has significant adverse effects and high costs, it is essential to minimize unnecessary treatment. Therefore, Test B, with its higher specificity, would be the better choice to avoid false positives and unnecessary treatment, despite its lower sensitivity. This is particularly important when the consequences of a false positive could lead to unnecessary treatment and its associated risks.
